Under previous tax law, income from pass-through entities (i.e., sole proprietorships, partnerships, limited liability companies, and S corporations) were taxed as ordinary income to individual owners. Under the new tax law, owners may be permitted to deduct up to 20 percent of their “qualified business income” from pass-through entities on their individual income tax return from the total amount of income that is “passed through” to them.

  Corporations who issue Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) financial statements need to assess accruals for income taxes under ASC 740 as a result of the tax reform provisions. For calendar-year taxpayers, the impact of the law changes will need to be reflected in the Dec. 31, 2017, GAAP financial statements. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are valued at the anticipated tax rate in which the temporary differences are expected to reverse. With the corporate tax rate reduction to 21 percent, companies will need to remeasure their deferred tax assets and liabilities using the new, lower rate. The impact of the rate change will be reflected in the company’s income statement in continuing operations. Choice of Business Entity  New Law 

  Technology companies are generally either structured as an LLC or C corporation. Most technology companies begin with capital funding from founders, family, friends, and angel investors. An LLC structure provides investors the additional benefit of passing start-up losses through to the owners as ordinary losses, which may be deductible. When the companies begin accessing capital from more institutional investors or venture capital firms, many entities convert to C corporations. The new legislation could have an impact on entity choice for technology companies.

ceramic.title: Automated Support Calculators & True Income | Burch Shepard Family Law Group
ceramic.snippet:
Business owners in Newport Beach and across Orange County often operate through S corporations, LLCs, partnerships, or professional corporations. Each structure gives flexibility in how money flows to the owner. Some income appears as W-2 wages, some as distributions, some as reimbursements, and some as business-paid personal expenses. A tax return is designed to minimize taxable income within legal limits, not to show the full economic benefit available to the owner.

 Latent defects in disclosures show up in several ways. Business owners might provide corporate tax returns without the full set of schedules, or they may omit K-1s that show pass-through income. There may be a profit and loss statement, but no general ledger that would expose personal expenses booked as business costs.

  In a typical high-asset case, the first calculator run may rely only on W-2 wages and the net income listed on business returns. That gives us a baseline. Next, we gather deeper documentation: detailed general ledgers, bank statements, credit card statements, K-1s, and loan records between the business and the owner. We review these for personal expenses routed through the business, patterns of distributions, and any significant lifestyle spending that is inconsistent with claimed income. Each identified item can become an add-back to income for support purposes.

 Certain practical steps can help protect you. Gathering the right documents is critical. These often include corporate or partnership tax returns, K-1s, profit and loss statements, balance sheets, general ledgers, and bank statements for business and personal accounts. For contractors and commissioned earners, a multi-year history of invoices, commission statements, and bonus documentation can be very important. The more complete the picture, the easier it is to test and correct the income figure in the calculator.

jina.snippet:
Section 304 can be interpreted to allow multinational corporations to shift and often generate basis using intercompany sales, improperly increasing losses that can be recognized to offset US tax liability.

### The Problem

Section 304 was initially conceived as an anti-abuse measure to prevent corporations from paying disguised dividends. But its original purpose has been contorted, and it now facilitates several problematic transactional structures that corporate groups use to shift basis between related corporations. Mechanically, section 304 generally recharacterizes certain intercompany stock sales into intercompany dividends through a deemed issuance and redemption transaction. Depending on the tax strategy of an applicable multinational group, these dividends may be designed to consolidate previously taxed earnings and profits (PTEP) and corresponding basis amongst controlled foreign corporations or, in a more aggressive variant, to generate an artificially high and uneconomic stock basis. The basis shifted or created in these transactions can then be harvested as a loss.

jina.title: How to Change Business Ownership in California: A Step-by-Step Guide
jina.snippet:
Changing business ownership in California generally requires reviewing the entity's governing documents, drafting and signing a transfer or purchase agreement, updating internal records such as the operating agreement or bylaws, and filing an updated Statement of Information with the Secretary of State. The exact steps differ depending on whether the business is an LLC, corporation, or partnership, but every transfer should be documented in writing and reported to the appropriate state and tax agencies to avoid disputes or compliance penalties down the road.

![Image 1: How to Change Business Ownership in California](https://omnilawpc.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/How-to-Change-Business-Ownership-in-California-768x432.webp)

At a glance, a compliant ownership change typically involves:

*   Reviewing the operating agreement, bylaws, or partnership agreement for transfer restrictions
*   Obtaining written consent from remaining owners when required
*   Drafting a purchase, transfer, or assignment agreement
*   Updating ownership records, cap tables, or membership certificates
*   Filing an amended Statement of Information with the California Secretary of State
*   Notifying the IRS, Franchise Tax Board, and any licensing agencies of the change

## **What Does Changing Business Ownership Mean in California?**

Changing business ownership refers to any transaction that shifts who holds equity, membership interest, or voting control in a company. This can happen through a sale of the entire business, a partial transfer of shares or membership units, the addition of a new partner, or the departure of an existing owner through retirement, death, or a negotiated buyout. Unlike simply changing a business name or address, an ownership change usually affects tax reporting, banking authority, and legal liability, so it needs to be handled with the same care as forming the entity in the first place. keenable.title: 26 CFR 1.382-2T -- Definition of ownership change under section 382, as amended by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (temporary).
keenable.snippet:
(a) *Ownership change* —
(1) *In general.* A corporation is a new loss corporation and thus subject to limitation under section 382 only if an ownership change has occurred with respect to such corporation. An ownership change occurs with respect to a corporation if it is a loss corporation on a testing date and, immediately after the close of the testing date, the percentage of stock of the corporation owned by one or more 5-percent shareholders has increased by more than 50 percentage points over the lowest percentage of stock of such corporation owned by such shareholders at any time during the testing period. See paragraph (a)(2)(i) of this section for the definition of testing date. See paragraph (d) of this section for the definition of testing period. See § 1.382-2(a)(1) and paragraph (f)(3) of this section for the respective definition of loss corporation and new loss corporation. See paragraph (g) of this section for the definition of 5-percent shareholder.

(e) *Owner shift and equity structure shift* —
(1) *Owner shift* —
(i) *Defined.* For purposes of this section, an owner shift is any change in the ownership of the stock of a loss corporation that affects the percentage of such stock owned by any 5-percent shareholder. See paragraph (g) of this section for the definition of a 5-percent shareholder. An owner shift includes, but is not limited to, the following transactions:
(A) A purchase of disposition of loss corporation stock by a 5-percent shareholder,
(B) A section 351 exchange that affects the percentage of stock owned by a 5-percent shareholder,
(C) A redemption or a recapitalization that affects the percentage of stock owned by a 5-percent shareholder,
(D) An issuance of loss corporation stock that affects the percentage of stock owned by a 5-percent shareholder, and
(E) An equity structure shift that affects the percentage of stock owned by a 5-percent shareholder.

linkup.snippet:
Section 382 caps a loss corporation's ability to use prior NOLs once ownership shifts by more than 50 percentage points over the testing period.  
An owner shift under Section 382 of the Internal Revenue Code is any transaction that changes the percentage of a loss corporation’s stock held by a five-percent shareholder. When these shifts accumulate beyond a 50-percentage-point increase over a rolling three-year window, the corporation’s ability to use its [net operating loss carryforwards](https://legalclarity.org/how-the-net-operating-loss-carryforward-works/) and certain other tax attributes becomes sharply limited.
An equity structure shift is a related but narrower concept. It covers most [tax-free reorganizations under Section 368](https://legalclarity.org/what-are-the-tax-free-corporate-reorganization-rules/) involving the loss corporation, with the exception of certain divisive and mere-formality reorganizations (specifically D, G, and F reorganizations in most cases).[2](javascript:void%280%29)eCFR. [26 CFR 1.382-2T – Definition of Ownership Change Under Section 382](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-26/section-1.382-2) In practice, any equity structure shift that changes a five-percent shareholder’s percentage also qualifies as an owner shift, so the two concepts overlap heavily. The distinction matters mainly for the testing date mechanics: an equity structure shift can trigger a testing date even if no individual stock trade occurred.
A loss corporation must attach a statement to its income tax return for any year in which an owner shift, equity structure shift, or ownership change occurs. A Section 382 statement is a narrative disclosure that a loss corporation must attach to its income tax return whenever an ownership change occurs, reporting the change event and the resulting annual cap on pre-change net operating losses (NOLs) and other tax attributes. Treasury Regulation § 1.382-11(a) prescribes the required content, and while the regulation itself specifies only a handful of mandatory items, the underlying calculations demand significant supporting detail. The filing obligation arises when the loss corporation experiences an “ownership change” as defined in Section 382. A Section 382 statement is a disclosure filed with a company’s federal income tax return to report a significant change in ownership to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). This filing is required when a company with accumulated net operating losses (NOLs) or other tax attributes experiences an “ownership change.” The purpose of the filing is linked to Section 382 of the Internal Revenue Code, which restricts a company’s ability to use past losses to offset future income after such a change. The statement provides the IRS with data to verify the corporation’s calculation of its annual limitation on using these pre-change tax benefits and serves as the official record of the event.

## Determining if a Statement is Required

The requirement to file a Section 382 statement hinges on whether a corporation is a “loss corporation” and if it has undergone an “ownership change.” A loss corporation is any company possessing tax attributes like NOL carryforwards, certain unrealized built-in losses, or tax credit carryforwards. If a business has a history of losses that it can carry forward to reduce future tax bills, it meets the first part of this definition.

An ownership change is a technical event defined under the tax code. It occurs if the percentage of stock owned by one or more “5-percent shareholders” increases by more than 50 percentage points over the lowest percentage of stock owned by those shareholders during a defined “testing period.” A 5-percent shareholder is any individual or entity that directly or indirectly owns five percent or more of the corporation’s stock. The testing period is generally the three-year period ending on the day of any shift in ownership.

seltz.title: What Are the Different Ownership Tests for Tax and Accounting?
seltz.snippet:
Ownership tests are fundamental structural mechanisms used across US tax law, financial accounting, and regulatory compliance to determine control and affiliation. These tests establish legal thresholds that trigger significant consequences, such as limiting tax benefits or mandating financial reporting requirements.

Modern corporate structures often feature complex layers of equity, debt, and contractual arrangements, making simple majority voting insufficient for defining control. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB), and the Department of Labor (DOL) each employ distinct, hyperspecific tests tailored to their regulatory goals. Understanding these specific percentage thresholds and structural definitions is paramount for effective financial planning and compliance.

## Ownership Tests for Limiting Tax Attributes (Section 382)

Corporations holding Net Operating Losses (NOLs) and other valuable tax attributes must adhere to the stringent ownership tests outlined in Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 382. This statute is designed to prevent “trafficking” in tax losses, where a profitable company acquires a loss corporation solely to utilize the existing NOLs. The application of Section 382 is triggered by an “ownership change” that occurs over a specific testing period.

An ownership change is defined as a cumulative increase of more than 50 percentage points in the ownership of the loss corporation’s stock by one or more “5-percent shareholders” over the look-back window. The look-back window, known as the “testing period,” generally encompasses the three-year period preceding the testing date. A testing date is any date on which the corporation experiences an “owner shift” or an “equity structure shift.”

These shifts are the two primary mechanisms that mandate a recalculation of the cumulative ownership change.

ultimate.title: 26 CFR 1.382-2T -- Definition of ownership change under section 382, as amended by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (temporary).
ultimate.snippet:
(a) *Ownership change* —
(1) *In general.* A corporation is a new loss corporation and thus subject to limitation under section 382 only if an ownership change has occurred with respect to such corporation. An ownership change occurs with respect to a corporation if it is a loss corporation on a testing date and, immediately after the close of the testing date, the percentage of stock of the corporation owned by one or more 5-percent shareholders has increased by more than 50 percentage points over the lowest percentage of stock of such corporation owned by such shareholders at any time during the testing period. See paragraph (a)(2)(i) of this section for the definition of testing date. See paragraph (d) of this section for the definition of testing period. See § 1.382-2(a)(1) and paragraph (f)(3) of this section for the respective definition of loss corporation and new loss corporation. See paragraph (g) of this section for the definition of 5-percent shareholder.

(e) *Owner shift and equity structure shift* —
(1) *Owner shift* —
(i) *Defined.* For purposes of this section, an owner shift is any change in the ownership of the stock of a loss corporation that affects the percentage of such stock owned by any 5-percent shareholder. See paragraph (g) of this section for the definition of a 5-percent shareholder. An owner shift includes, but is not limited to, the following transactions:
(A) A purchase of disposition of loss corporation stock by a 5-percent shareholder,
(B) A section 351 exchange that affects the percentage of stock owned by a 5-percent shareholder,
(C) A redemption or a recapitalization that affects the percentage of stock owned by a 5-percent shareholder,
(D) An issuance of loss corporation stock that affects the percentage of stock owned by a 5-percent shareholder, and
(E) An equity structure shift that affects the percentage of stock owned by a 5-percent shareholder.
